design_detail: Mendelian randomization with individual-participant data pooled from 56 studies (261 991 participants of European descent), using a single instrument: carriage of the A-allele of ADH1B rs1229984, a variant of an alcohol-metabolising enzyme, analysed as a dominant trait (carriers of one or two A-alleles, on average about 7% of participants, against GG homozygotes). Genotype associations with alcohol traits, cardiovascular biomarkers, lifestyle factors, coronary heart disease (primary outcome), stroke and type 2 diabetes were estimated within each study and combined by fixed-effect meta-analysis (random effects as a check), overall and within strata of self-reported intake (0, >0 to <21 and ≥21 UK units/week; for coronary heart disease the middle stratum was split at 7 units/week). No instrumental-variable estimate of the effect of a given amount of alcohol was computed. The studies were not found by a systematic search: the authors approached population-based studies genotyped on the IBC CardioChip array, genetic study groups they had worked with (offering new genotyping) and a few studies that had published on the variant; 56 of 59 took part. The paper calls them epidemiological studies; their individual designs are listed in an appendix that was not read, and coronary events and strokes included both incident and prevalent cases. A conventional analysis of self-reported intake against risk factors (131 490 people, 28 studies) is reported only in the appendix. Labelled prospective-cohort and appraised with ROBINS-E under the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization of pooled cohorts, because the protocol names no instrument for this design.
can_establish: Whether people carrying an allele that lowers drinking (about 17% fewer self-reported units per week, more abstention, less binge drinking) have lower blood pressure, inflammatory markers, adiposity and odds of coronary heart disease than non-carriers, in a comparison that assignment of genotype at conception protects from confounding by lifestyle and from illness changing drinking, provided the variant affects these outcomes only through alcohol.
cannot_establish: What a given amount of alcohol does, or the shape of the dose-response at low intake (one binary variant shifts intake proportionally, no instrumental-variable estimate was made, and the strata are defined by self-reported drinking, which the genotype itself changes); that cutting down helps light drinkers in particular (the light and moderate strata each have intervals that include no difference); and that the variant acts only through alcohol (carriers who reported not drinking also had lower blood pressure, interleukin-6 and body mass index).

sample.recruitment: Pooled studies identified through collaboration, not a systematic search: population-based studies genotyped on the IBC CardioChip array, genetic study groups that had worked with the authors (some genotyped anew), and a small number of European-descent studies that had published on this variant; the public CARDIoGRAMplusC4D data did not include the variant. Of 59 studies approached, 56 were included: INTERHEART and INTERSTROKE declined because of overlap with other projects, and CoLaus was excluded because the variant had not been genotyped directly (Methods › Formation of the consortium; Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Participants of European descent with data on rs1229984 genotype, age, sex and at least one outcome; not every study contributed to every analysis, because the variables collected differed (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph; appendix figure S2, not read).
sample.demographics: 48% women; mean age per study 58 years (study means ranged from 26 to 75). Median alcohol intake by study is given only in appendix table S4 (not read) (Results, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable to a pooled genetic analysis. Of the 261 991 participants, 168 731 (from 46 studies) entered the coronary heart disease analysis. The analysis by drinking status covered 150 507 participants with 16 013 of the 20 259 coronary events, so about 4246 events (21%) had no usable alcohol data (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2).
sample.selection_effects: Studies entered because they had genotyped the variant on one array or belonged to the authors' network, mainly with unpublished genetic data, which the authors argue protects against publication bias. Coronary events and strokes included prevalent cases, so people who died before a study enrolled them are missing; if the genotype affected survival after an event, the odds ratios could be biased (not addressed). Only people of European descent were analysed. The analyses within drinking strata compare carriers and non-carriers selected on self-reported drinking, a variable the genotype affects; the authors checked only that lifestyle factors were not differentially associated with the genotype across strata (Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and lifestyle factors).

exposure.measurement: Instrument: rs1229984 genotyped directly in every study (median call rate 98.8%; platforms and Hardy-Weinberg tests in appendix table S1, not read). Alcohol: self-reported weekly volume in UK units derived from each study's questionnaire (1 UK unit = 10 mL or 7.9 g ethanol = 0.57 US units), drinking status (drinkers v non-drinkers), the study- and sex-specific top third of intake, and binge drinking (definitions in appendix table S2, not read); γ-glutamyltransferase as a marker of heavy drinking (Methods › Alcohol traits).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Instrument relevance: carriers reported 17.2% fewer units per week (95% CI 15.6% to 18.9%; 46 studies, 218 969 people; P=5.5×10−76; I2 64%), were less often in their study's top third of intake (OR 0.70, 0.68 to 0.73) or binge drinkers (0.78, 0.73 to 0.84), higher odds of reporting abstention (1.27, 1.21 to 1.34), and 1.8% lower γ-glutamyltransferase (−3.4% to −0.3%) (Table 1). The proportional reduction looked constant across the range of intake (appendix figures S5 and S6, not read). No F statistic is reported. Strata used: none (0 units/week), light to moderate (>0 to <21) and heavy (≥21, about 166 g ethanol/week by the editors' conversion); for coronary heart disease, light (>0 to <7), moderate (≥7 to <21) and heavy (≥21).
exposure.polysubstance: Smoking was examined as a possible confounder of the instrument: carriers had slightly higher odds of ever smoking (OR 1.06, 1.02 to 1.09), opposite in direction to the observational smoking-drinking association, and no difference in cigarettes per day, pack-years or cotinine (Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and lifestyle factors). Other drug use was not reported.

comparison.controls: Non-carriers (GG homozygotes) in the same studies, compared within each study and then pooled. In the stratified analyses the comparison is between carriers and non-carriers within the same self-reported drinking category; the non-drinker stratum is people reporting 0 units/week, and whether former drinkers were separated is defined study by study in appendix table S2 (not read); the authors note that long-term non-drinkers are hard to classify from questionnaires (Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph). The main text reports no conventional analysis of self-reported intake against cardiovascular events.
comparison.matching: None needed for the genetic comparison; estimates are crude within-study contrasts (Figure 1 legend), with adjustment for principal components of ancestry where available as a sensitivity analysis.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Genotype is fixed at conception, so premorbid differences between carriers and non-carriers are expected only through population structure or neighbouring variants. Checks: adjustment for principal components in studies with genome-wide data did not change the estimates (appendix figures S15-S16); no linkage disequilibrium with known cardiovascular genome-wide loci, tested in Whitehall II only (table S11). Carriers had slightly more years of education (0.04 SD, 0.01 to 0.08), which the authors say needs further study.

outcomes.instruments: Coronary heart disease (primary): incident and prevalent, fatal and non-fatal events. Stroke of all subtypes, incident and prevalent, with ischaemic stroke separately in a subsample. Type 2 diabetes: prevalent cases, except one nested case-cohort with incident cases. Study-specific definitions are in appendix table S3 (not read). Biomarkers: systolic blood pressure, hypertension, body mass index, waist circumference, interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, non-HDL and HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, apolipoprotein A1, and eight further traits (carotid intima-media thickness, electrocardiographic left ventricular hypertrophy, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, factor VII, fasting glucose, NT-proBNP, lipoprotein(a)).
outcomes.validity_norms: Outcome definitions and ascertainment varied by study; no central adjudication is described in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Odds ratio of the outcome in carriers against non-carriers (log odds ratios pooled across studies); mean or percentage differences for continuous traits.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 22 counts the four clinical outcomes and the 18 cardiovascular traits named in the main text; the paper also reports five alcohol traits, at least six lifestyle factors, stratified analyses in three or four drinking categories, and 58 plus 48 exploratory subgroup comparisons, all judged at P<0.05 two-sided.

analysis.effect_sizes: [Genetic; carriers v non-carriers; fixed-effect pooled] Coronary heart disease OR 0.90 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.96; 46 studies, 20 259 events in 168 731 people; I2 17%; P=0.001); in the four studies with ≥1000 events (8374 events) 0.81 (0.72 to 0.91; I2 0%). By self-reported drinking (UK units/week): non-drinkers 0.98 (0.88 to 1.10; 5883 events in 43 029); drinkers 0.86 (0.78 to 0.94; 10 130 in 107 478); test of difference P=0.095; light (>0 to <7) 0.90 (0.79 to 1.02; 4686 in 47 246), moderate (≥7 to <21) 0.89 (0.75 to 1.06; 3222 in 33 772), heavy (≥21) 0.97 (0.76 to 1.24; 1919 in 16 225); trend P=0.83 (Figure 2). Stroke 0.98 (0.90 to 1.07; 10 164 events in 145 063); ischaemic stroke 0.83 (0.72 to 0.95; subset); type 2 diabetes 1.02 (0.95 to 1.09) (Figure 3). Biomarkers: systolic blood pressure −0.88 mm Hg (−1.19 to −0.56); hypertension OR 0.94 (0.91 to 0.98; 104 570 cases); interleukin-6 −5.2%; C-reactive protein −3.4%; body mass index −0.17 kg/m2; waist −0.34 cm; non-HDL cholesterol −0.03 mmol/L; triglycerides +1.6%; HDL cholesterol −0.004 mmol/L (−0.012 to 0.003) (Table 2). Random-effects estimates were similar. No absolute risks and no instrumental-variable estimates are reported.
analysis.covariates: None in the main genetic contrasts (crude, within study); principal components of ancestry in the studies that had them, as a sensitivity analysis.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is reported. A standard analysis protocol was sent to the participating studies (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph); it is not published with the main text (appendix not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: The stratum-specific coronary estimates and the test of non-drinkers against drinkers (P=0.095) appear only in Figure 2; the text gives the non-drinker and drinker estimates without that test. The Methods describe three drinking strata (0, >0 to <21, ≥21 units/week); the coronary analysis split the middle one at 7 units/week. Several subgroup results are stated to be available on request rather than shown.
analysis.power: Not reported. The authors attribute the weak coronary association in heavy drinkers (OR 0.97, 0.76 to 1.24; 1919 events) to few events and call the number of strokes an important limitation (Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of the study, 4th paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Carriers of the intake-lowering ADH1B allele drank about 17% less and had slightly lower blood pressure, inflammatory markers, adiposity and non-HDL cholesterol, and 10% lower odds of coronary heart disease (OR 0.90, 0.84 to 0.96); there was no association with all stroke or type 2 diabetes, and lower odds of ischaemic stroke in a subset. Within drinking strata the coronary odds ratios were 0.90 (light), 0.89 (moderate) and 0.97 (heavy), each with an interval including 1, and the difference between non-drinkers (0.98) and drinkers (0.86) had P=0.095. In people reporting no drinking, carriers still had lower systolic blood pressure (−0.80 mm Hg), interleukin-6 (−7.15%) and body mass index (−0.21), about as much as light-to-moderate drinkers (Figure 1).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that reducing alcohol, "even for light to moderate drinkers, is beneficial for cardiovascular health" (Abstract, Conclusions); the summary box on what the study adds says the lower risk held at all levels of drinking, while the Discussion's section on the meaning of the study says such reductions may be beneficial. Gaps: (1) the statement about light-to-moderate drinkers rests on stratified estimates that are each compatible with no difference and on a non-significant heterogeneity test (P=0.83), which shows no detectable difference between strata, not equal benefit; (2) stratifying on self-reported drinking, which the genotype changes, can itself create bias, which the authors examined only through lifestyle factors; (3) the Discussion states that associations with the traits were null or much weaker in non-drinkers, as expected if the variant works only through alcohol, but Figure 1 shows associations of similar size in non-drinkers for systolic blood pressure, interleukin-6, body mass index and C-reactive protein, pointing either to misclassified former or occasional drinkers or to a pathway other than current drinking, which the paper does not discuss; (4) a single variant shifting intake by about 17% cannot show what happens below a given intake or compare light drinking with none, and no causal effect per unit of alcohol was estimated; (5) light to moderate here means >0 to <21 UK units/week (up to about 166 g ethanol), self-reported. The conclusion that the observational J-shape reflects residual confounding or selection bias (Discussion › Meaning of the study) is a reasonable inference, but the paper tests neither explanation.

timeline.event: This study: by the authors' account the first Mendelian randomization analysis large enough to detect an association of an alcohol-lowering genotype with coronary heart disease events (Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses in relation to other studies, 1st paragraph).

Millwood et al. (China Kadoorie Biobank; ALDH2 rs671 and ADH1B rs1229984): genotype-predicted male intake was associated log-linearly with ischaemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage but not with myocardial infarction (RR 0.96 per 280 g/week); those authors describe their rs1229984-only coronary result as consistent with this study.

Mukamal, Stampfer and Rimm, "Genetic instrumental variable analysis: time to call Mendelian randomization what it is" (Eur J Epidemiol), listed in the project's DOI list as a critique of the Mendelian randomization studies of alcohol and cardiovascular disease; not read for this card. Two of its three authors (K Mukamal, E Rimm) are coauthors of this study.

Larsson et al. (two-sample Mendelian randomization with up to 94 variants, European ancestry): genetically predicted drinking associated with stroke (OR 1.27 per SD of log drinks/week) and borderline with coronary artery disease (1.16, 1.00 to 1.36), attenuated after adjustment for smoking liability; rs1229984 alone was associated with coronary artery disease in a dataset with about three times this study's coronary cases, by Larsson and colleagues' account.

Biddinger et al. (UK Biobank; variants associated with alcohol use disorder): linear Mendelian randomization OR for coronary artery disease 1.38 (1.10 to 1.74) per SD of genetically predicted intake, and nonlinear analyses that those authors read as risk rising from the lowest intakes.

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of the coronary result (a genotype that lowers drinking goes with fewer coronary events) was seen again in later European-ancestry Mendelian randomization (Larsson et al., 2020, for rs1229984; Biddinger et al., 2022), but not for myocardial infarction in the east Asian two-variant analysis (Millwood et al., 2019). For stroke the studies differ: this one found no association with all stroke, while the later ones found higher genetically predicted intake associated with more stroke, especially intracerebral haemorrhage. Whether cutting down benefits light drinkers is the contested part: this design cannot show it, and the stratified estimates the abstract relies on are imprecise and open to selection bias. Millwood et al. share two authors with this study (M V Holmes, G Davey Smith), so the two are not fully independent.

The paper states that the funders had no role in design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit (Funding of individuals; Funding of studies; Statement of independence from funders).
funding.declared_conflicts: One author (J Whittaker) declared being 90% employed by GlaxoSmithKline and owning GlaxoSmithKline shares. All other coauthors declared no support for the submitted work, no financial relationships in the previous three years with organisations that might have an interest in it, and no other relevant relationships or activities (Competing interests). No ties to the alcohol industry are declared.
funding.affiliations_note: A consortium of more than 150 authors from the contributing studies. The author list includes K Mukamal and E Rimm, two of the three authors of the 2019 critique of Mendelian randomization evidence on alcohol named in the DOI list. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A Mendelian randomization study of incident coronary events in a population where genotype produces large absolute differences in intake down to near zero (as with ALDH2 in east Asia), using several independent alcohol variants, nonlinear methods whose assumptions are checked, and biomarker-verified non-drinkers to test whether the variant acts outside alcohol. A long-term randomized trial of light drinking against abstention with cardiovascular events as the outcome, which the authors consider not feasible, would answer the light-drinking question directly.

domains.note: Instrument independence: genotype is assigned at conception; adjustment for principal components of ancestry did not change the estimates where available, and no linkage disequilibrium with known cardiovascular loci was found (one cohort). An HDL association confined to northern European studies raised the possibility of population structure, which principal-component adjustment did not confirm. Small imbalances: education (+0.04 SD) and ever smoking (OR 1.06, in the direction that would not produce the protective result). Exclusion restriction (no other path from variant to outcome): ADH1B is an alcohol-metabolising enzyme, so a path outside drinking is less likely than for behavioural variants, and the coronary association was null in self-reported non-drinkers (0.98, 0.88 to 1.10); but its difference from drinkers was not significant (P=0.095), and in non-drinkers the variant was still associated with lower systolic blood pressure, interleukin-6 and body mass index (Figure 1). Pleiotropy-robust methods are not possible with one variant.

Relevance: strong (17.2% fewer units per week, P=5.5×10−76, with consistent effects on abstention, binge drinking and γ-glutamyltransferase), although no F statistic is given and only about 7% of participants carry the allele. Shape at low intake: the instrument shifts intake proportionally and cannot show what happens at specific low intakes; the paper deliberately computes no causal effect per unit. Intake itself is self-reported with heterogeneous questionnaires, which matters for the strata.

Selection into the pooled data: studies chosen by genotyping platform and collaboration rather than by search, European descent only, and prevalent as well as incident events (survivors only). For the stratified estimates the risk is high: carriers and non-carriers are compared within categories of self-reported drinking that the genotype itself influences; the authors examined lifestyle factors across strata (no differential association) but not other consequences of this conditioning.
Not applicable in the usual sense: the instrument is fixed at conception, and later changes in drinking are part of what it captures.

Studies contributed according to the variables they had collected, which is unlikely to depend on genotype. About a fifth of coronary events lacked the alcohol data needed for the stratified analysis (editors' arithmetic), which affects only the stratified estimates.

Study-specific definitions of coronary heart disease, stroke and diabetes, mixing incident and prevalent and fatal and non-fatal events, without central adjudication. Misclassification is unlikely to depend on genotype and would mainly dilute associations.

No registered plan; many outcomes, strata and subgroups without correction; the coronary analysis split a stratum described in the Methods; stratified biomarker results that contradict the Discussion's account of non-drinkers are shown in Figure 1 but described inaccurately in the text.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: For the main result, the pooled association of the alcohol-lowering ADH1B genotype with lower odds of coronary heart disease (OR 0.90) and with lower blood pressure and adiposity, the design is well protected against the confounding that affects conventional studies, the instrument is strong and tied to alcohol metabolism, and outcome misclassification would bias towards no association; the remaining concerns are pleiotropy (biomarker associations in non-drinkers), the choice of studies and the inclusion of prevalent cases. The stratified estimates, which carry the abstract's message about light to moderate drinkers, are at high risk of bias from conditioning on self-reported drinking and are imprecise. Design label and instrument follow the round brief's rule for Mendelian randomization (the protocol is silent). Cite this card for: genetic evidence that a variant lowering alcohol intake is associated with lower coronary risk and lower blood pressure in people of European descent. Do not cite it for: a benefit of cutting down in light drinkers specifically, a dose-response or threshold, the absence of any protective effect at low intake, or stroke (null overall; ischaemic stroke only in a subset).

key_findings.finding: 56 of 59 approached studies took part, giving 261 991 participants of European descent (48% women; mean age per study 58, range 26-75) with 20 259 coronary heart disease events, 10 164 strokes (4339 ischaemic) and 14 549 type 2 diabetes cases; all studies genotyped rs1229984 directly (median call rate 98.8%).
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Genotype properties

key_findings.finding: Instrument and alcohol (carriers v non-carriers): 17.2% fewer UK units per week (95% CI 15.6% to 18.9%; 46 studies, 218 969 people; P=5.5×10−76; I2 64%); top third of intake OR 0.70 (0.68 to 0.73); binge drinking 0.78 (0.73 to 0.84); self-reported abstention 1.27 (1.21 to 1.34); γ-glutamyltransferase −1.84% (−3.40 to −0.26). One UK unit is 10 mL or 7.9 g of ethanol.
key_findings.locator: Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and alcohol consumption, 1st paragraph; Table 1 and its footnotes

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers (carriers v non-carriers, all participants): systolic blood pressure −0.88 mm Hg (−1.19 to −0.56; 48 studies, 227 559 people); hypertension OR 0.94 (0.91 to 0.98; 104 570 cases); body mass index −0.17 kg/m2 (−0.24 to −0.10); waist −0.34 cm (−0.58 to −0.10); interleukin-6 −5.15% (−7.82 to −2.40); C-reactive protein −3.40% (−5.68 to −1.05); non-HDL cholesterol −0.03 mmol/L (−0.05 to −0.01); triglycerides +1.61% (0.66 to 2.57); HDL cholesterol −0.004 mmol/L (−0.012 to 0.003; P=0.259).
key_findings.locator: Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and cardiovascular biomarkers, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Coronary heart disease, carriers v non-carriers: OR 0.90 (0.84 to 0.96; I2 17%; 46 studies, 20 259 events in 168 731 people; P=0.001); in the four studies with at least 1000 events (8374 events) 0.81 (0.72 to 0.91; I2 0%).
key_findings.locator: Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and cardiovascular events, 1st paragraph; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Coronary heart disease by self-reported drinking (UK units/week; carriers v non-carriers within each stratum): non-drinkers OR 0.98 (0.88 to 1.10; 31 studies, 5883 events in 43 029); drinkers 0.86 (0.78 to 0.94; 40 studies, 10 130 in 107 478); P for heterogeneity between the two 0.095. Light (>0 to <7) 0.90 (0.79 to 1.02; 4686 in 47 246); moderate (≥7 to <21) 0.89 (0.75 to 1.06; 3222 in 33 772); heavy (≥21) 0.97 (0.76 to 1.24; 1919 in 16 225); P for trend across the three 0.828 (meta-regression).
key_findings.locator: Figure 2; Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and cardiovascular events, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Stratum values and the P=0.095 test are printed beside the forest plot in Figure 2 (an image), read from the full-size figure image; the text gives only the non-drinker, drinker and P=0.83 results. None of the three drinker-category intervals excludes 1.

key_findings.finding: Stroke and diabetes: all stroke OR 0.98 (0.90 to 1.07; 35 studies, 10 164 events in 145 063); ischaemic stroke 0.83 (0.72 to 0.95; subset with subtype data); type 2 diabetes 1.02 (0.95 to 1.09; 14 549 cases in 178 388). In non-drinkers, stroke 1.12 (0.98 to 1.28) and diabetes 1.09 (0.98 to 1.21); in drinkers 0.95 (0.83 to 1.07) and 0.97 (0.86 to 1.09). The authors call the small number of strokes and the pooling of stroke subtypes an important limitation, and say the ischaemic-stroke result, from a subset of studies, requires replication.
key_findings.locator: Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and cardiovascular events, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3; Discussion › Strengths and weaknesses of the study, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Stratified stroke and diabetes values are printed in Figure 3 (an image), read from the full-size figure image.

key_findings.finding: Biomarkers by drinking stratum (none; light to moderate, >0 to <21; heavy, ≥21 UK units/week): systolic blood pressure −0.80 (−1.41 to −0.19), −0.68 (−1.09 to −0.26), −1.70 (−2.55 to −0.86) mm Hg; interleukin-6 −7.15% (−11.49 to −2.64), −7.24% (−10.69 to −3.65), −12.45% (−20.71 to −3.35); body mass index −0.21 (−0.35 to −0.06), −0.11 (−0.21 to −0.02), −0.77 (−0.93 to −0.62); C-reactive protein −3.32% (−7.42 to 0.95), −3.52% (−6.54 to −0.40), −19.10% (−24.42 to −13.41); non-HDL cholesterol +0.03 (0.00 to 0.07), −0.02 (−0.05 to 0.00), −0.25 (−0.30 to −0.19) mmol/L; waist −0.32 (−0.77 to 0.13), +0.16 (−0.16 to 0.48), −1.27 (−1.87 to −0.66) cm; hypertension (odds ratio) 0.95 (0.89 to 1.02), 0.98 (0.93 to 1.03), 0.89 (0.81 to 0.99), trend P = 0.197 (systolic blood pressure trend P = 0.07), so the lower odds of hypertension were clear only in heavy drinkers.
key_findings.note: Values printed beside the forest plots in Figure 1 (an image), read from the full-size figure image. In non-drinkers the associations with systolic blood pressure, interleukin-6, body mass index and C-reactive protein are about as large as in light-to-moderate drinkers, contrary to the Discussion's description (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: HDL cholesterol: no overall association; in the heaviest drinking category carriers had higher HDL (+0.04 mmol/L, 0.02 to 0.06), opposite to what the observational association predicts; carriers in northern Europe had lower HDL (−0.04, −0.05 to −0.02); adjustment for principal components in non-northern studies did not change the null result.
key_findings.locator: Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and cardiovascular biomarkers, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lifestyle factors: no association of the variant with physical activity; ever smoking OR 1.06 (1.02 to 1.09), opposite in direction to the observational association; no association with cigarettes per day, pack-years or cotinine; years of education +0.04 SD (0.01 to 0.08); no differential association across drinking strata.
key_findings.locator: Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and lifestyle factors, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Adjustment for population structure did not alter the associations, and the variant was not in linkage disequilibrium with known genome-wide loci for cardiovascular traits; random-effects estimates were similar to fixed-effect ones.
key_findings.locator: Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and cardiovascular events, 3rd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: No instrumental-variable analysis was done, because available methods assume a linear exposure-outcome relation, which the authors say may not hold for alcohol and cardiovascular disease.

The Methods state that, if the observational U-shape were causal, carriers should have higher coronary risk among light-to-moderate drinkers (>0 to <21 units/week) and lower risk among heavy drinkers (≥21), and that the variant should have no or an attenuated effect in non-drinkers.
key_findings.note: No protocol or registration was published, so whether the expectation was set before the analysis cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says that for the traits associated with the variant overall, associations were null or substantially reduced in non-drinkers, as expected if the variant acts only through alcohol. Figure 1 shows associations in non-drinkers of about the same size as in light-to-moderate drinkers for systolic blood pressure (−0.80 v −0.68 mm Hg), interleukin-6 (−7.15% v −7.24%), body mass index (−0.21 v −0.11) and C-reactive protein (−3.32% v −3.52%).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion › Principal findings of study, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's main check of the no-other-path assumption is weaker than described: either self-reported non-drinkers include many former or occasional drinkers, or the variant affects these traits outside current drinking. Claims should not cite the non-drinker analysis as confirming the instrument.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the protective association "remained the same across all categories" of drinking, citing P=0.83 for heterogeneity, but the stratum estimates in Figure 2 (light 0.90, 0.79 to 1.02; moderate 0.89, 0.75 to 1.06; heavy 0.97, 0.76 to 1.24) each include 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: A non-significant heterogeneity test is presented as evidence of an equal effect; the benefit for light or moderate drinkers is not established by these estimates.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results describe the null coronary association in non-drinkers and the reduced odds in drinkers as consistent with the instrument acting through alcohol, without the formal test of their difference, which Figure 2 gives as P=0.095.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and cardiovascular events, 1st paragraph; Figure 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The difference between non-drinkers and drinkers that supports the exclusion assumption for coronary heart disease is not statistically established.

reporting_issues.issue: The stratified coronary analysis covers 16 013 of the 20 259 events (non-drinkers 5883 plus drinkers 10 130), and the three drinker categories sum to 9827 events and 97 243 people against 10 130 events and 107 478 people for all drinkers (editors' arithmetic from Figure 2); the text does not explain the missing events.
reporting_issues.consequence: About a fifth of coronary events, and some drinkers, are absent from the stratified estimates, which are therefore based on a subset of studies or participants that may differ from the whole.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion that reduction is beneficial even for light to moderate drinkers is stronger than the Discussion's corresponding sentence, which says such reductions may be beneficial.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract (Conclusions); Discussion › Meaning of the study
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline wording should not be carried into claims; the paper's own discussion is more tentative.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods specify three drinking strata (0, >0 to <21, ≥21 units/week) chosen to represent the U-shape; the coronary results are reported in four (with light and moderate split at 7 units/week), a subdivision introduced in the Results.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Statistical analysis, 5th paragraph; Results › Genetic association analysis › ADH1B and cardiovascular events, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the finer split is not prespecified, and it lowers the precision of each stratum estimate.
